idiom_name: std::function<void()> pairs stored in a history vector
implementation_notes: Modern C++ default: stop declaring a class per request and store std::function objects instead. The standard library documents std::function as a general-purpose polymorphic wrapper that can hold functions, lambdas, bind expressions and other function objects, so a command becomes a lambda capturing the receiver and the parameters by value; the invoker keeps the pair of forward and inverse actions, because a plain std::function<void()> cannot undo anything by itself. The classic hierarchy is still justified when requests must be extended outside the translation unit, when undo differs per request type, or when a stable serialised identity is required.
pitfalls: std::function requires copy-constructible targets; a move-only lambda needs C++23 std::move_only_function or the variant/visitor form instead.
Capturing by reference makes a queued or replayed command dangle once the scope ends; capture the receiver by pointer or weak handle and the parameters by value.
Large captures may force a heap allocation inside std::function; in hot paths a function_ref, a hand-written callable or the std::variant form avoids that traffic.

variants.name: Classic Command class hierarchy (GoF form)
variants.idiom_name: abstract Command base with execute()/undo() subclasses and a unique_ptr history
variants.implementation_notes: The book's structure written in C++: a polymorphic base declares execute() and undo(), each request is a subclass holding the receiver and its parameters, and the invoker owns them through std::unique_ptr. Choose it when the command set must be open for extension, when per-request undo logic needs its own state, or when the code base predates C++11 - it is the only realization here that supports heterogeneous extension through inheritance.
pitfalls: Raw Command* in the invoker leaks on every path that forgets a delete; own commands with std::unique_ptr unless something else has a longer lifetime.
Storing a reference to the receiver hides the lifetime dependency - if the receiver dies first the call is undefined behaviour, so prefer a weak handle or a registry lookup.
Deep hierarchies duplicate the inverse logic across siblings; keep per-request state inside the concrete command and let undo() operate on it.

variants.name: std::variant command set dispatched with std::visit
variants.idiom_name: std::variant<InsertText, DeleteRange> with a std::visit overload set
variants.implementation_notes: Command as data: the request set is a std::variant of small parameter structs, the invoker stores the variant itself and execution is std::visit over an overload set. cppreference documents std::visit as applying a callable to the variant held by the object, which is exactly a closed-world dispatch table: storage is contiguous, there is no vtable, commands are trivially copyable and serialisable, and adding a request type breaks compilation everywhere it must be handled - the deliberate trade for that closed-world guarantee.
pitfalls: The variant closes the command set: a new alternative must be handled by every visitor, and a missing branch shows up as a compile error or an unintended overload match.
A visitor written with a single generic lambda loses exhaustiveness; use an overload helper plus a static_assert so an unhandled alternative fails loudly.
Pushing commands copies the whole payload into the history; move them in and keep each alternative small, or store an index/offset representation.
